summary.text: Algebra is a branch of mathematics that deals with abstract systems called algebraic structures and with manipulating expressions within those systems.
It generalizes arithmetic by introducing variables, symbols for unknown or unspecified quantities, which make it possible to state general laws.
Elementary algebra is the form taught in schools, while abstract algebra goes further and studies structures such as groups, rings and fields.

paragraphs.heading: What algebra studies
paragraphs.text: Algebra is a branch of mathematics whose subject is algebraic structures and the operations used within them. An algebraic structure is a set of mathematical objects that is not empty, such as the integers, together with operations defined on it, such as addition and multiplication. Algebra asks what laws these structures obey and what kinds of them there are. It reaches well beyond itself, into geometry, topology, number theory and calculus, and also into logic and the empirical sciences.

paragraphs.heading: Arithmetic with letters
paragraphs.text: Algebra is often described as arithmetic made more general. Arithmetic works with operations like adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing on one particular kind of number, such as the real numbers. Algebra keeps those operations but also lets you use variables: symbols that stand for quantities that are unknown or left unspecified. Variables let you describe a relationship even when you do not know the exact values, and state laws that hold whatever numbers you choose.

paragraphs.heading: From one fact to a law
paragraphs.text: Take the statement 2 × 3 = 3 × 2. That is arithmetic, and it is true only for those two numbers. Swap the numbers for variables and you get a × b = b × a. Now the statement covers every possible pair of numbers, and it has a name: the commutative property of multiplication.

paragraphs.heading: Levels of abstraction
paragraphs.text: Elementary algebra, the kind taught in schools, is the first step up from arithmetic. It sticks to particular numbers and operations but adds variables, and it tries to find which values make a statement true by reshaping equations until a variable stands alone. Linear algebra deals with linear equations and with systems of them, looking for the values that satisfy every equation in a system at once. Abstract algebra is not tied to any one kind of number and studies structures such as groups, rings and fields, telling them apart by how many operations they have and by their axioms, the laws they obey. Universal algebra goes further still and looks at what algebraic structures have in common in general.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word algebra comes from the Arabic al-jabr, which first meant the surgical setting of broken bones. In the 9th century the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi gave it a mathematical meaning. He used it for a method of transforming equations and put it in the title of his treatise, later translated into Latin as Liber Algebrae et Almucabola. English borrowed the word in the 1500s, taking it from Italian, Spanish and medieval Latin.

paragraphs.heading: How algebra grew
paragraphs.text: In ancient times, algebraic methods were worked out to solve particular problems in subjects such as geometry. Al-Khwarizmi changed that by making algebra a discipline of its own, separate from geometry. Early mathematicians wrote out equations and their solutions in words and abbreviations, until a strict system of symbols was built in the 16th and 17th centuries. At first algebra meant the theory of equations, the craft of handling polynomial equations in order to solve them. In the mid-19th century it widened to take in many kinds of operations and structures, along with the axioms they follow.
